Thank you for joining this workshop at the Research Data Conference 2026. Your instructor [{{< var author >}}]({{< var author-url >}}), {{< var department >}}, {{< var institute >}}, is looking forward to meeting you.

We meet on {{< var session.datetime >}} ({{< var session.timezone-label >}}) in {{< var session.event-location >}}. Conference programme and venue: [{{< var session.event-location-directions >}}]({{< var session.event-location-directions >}}). Registration runs through the conference.

## {{< fa circle-info >}} Background

Git and GitHub are the connective tissue of reproducible, collaborative research, yet many researchers learn them through fragmented tutorials that stop short of the collaboration patterns that matter: branching, pull requests, review and merging. This workshop is delivered as if every participant were a learner, and the real audience is educators: data stewards, research software engineers and instructors who teach, or want to teach, similar material. You first experience a condensed version of the full course from the learner's seat, then switch to an educator lens to judge whether you could teach it in your own context. The course is published as an open educational resource.

## {{< fa graduation-cap >}} Prior knowledge

No experience with Git or GitHub is assumed, and no programming. The hands-on part runs in GitHub Desktop, which works for files of any kind. In the pre-course survey some of you said you work in R, some in Python and some do not programme. If you already use Git with another tool, bring that tool.

## {{< fa suitcase >}} What do I need to bring to the workshop?

-   a laptop with GitHub Desktop installed and its charger, connected to the conference wifi
-   a web browser (preferably Chrome or Firefox)
-   a pen and paper (we will be doing some drawings)
-   the pre-work below completed

[Prior to the workshop, there is some pre-work for you to do]{.highlight-yellow}. It keeps our two hours for the collaboration skills instead of setting up infrastructure.

## {{< fa circle-question >}} What do I need to prepare before the workshop?

-   [Step 1](pre-work/01-survey.html): Complete the pre-course survey by [**{{< var session.survey-deadline >}}**]{.highlight-yellow}.
-   [Step 2](pre-work/02-github-acc.html): Get an account for GitHub, if you have none.
-   [Step 3](pre-work/03-github-desktop.html): Install GitHub Desktop and sign in.
-   [Step 4](pre-work/04-email-privacy.html): Decide where your email address shows.
-   [Step 5](pre-work/05-setup-check.html): Do the setup check.
-   [Step 6](pre-work/06-your-repository.html): Create your own repository and make your first commit.

Steps 3 to 6 take about 60 minutes and are due by [**{{< var session.repository-deadline >}}**]{.highlight-yellow}. The hands-on part builds on the pre-work. Anyone who arrives without it sits with a prepared neighbour and follows on their laptop, and takes full part in the educator part of the workshop.

## {{< fa bullseye >}} Learning objectives

By the end of this workshop, participants will be able to:

1. **Collaboration patterns**: make a commit in a repository of their own and follow the path of a change through branch, pull request, review and merge.

2. **Instructional design**: evaluate how the workshop is built and taught (content, presentation, interaction, preparation) from an educator's perspective.

3. **Reuse**: assess whether they could reuse and adapt the material to teach Git and GitHub in their own setting.

Objectives 1 and 2 were updated after the abstract was submitted, to match the workshop as it runs on 20 November 2026.
